package_info.why_malicious: The package is part of a mass-flooding campaign that publishes hundreds of thousands of functionally useless or near-empty packages to npm, straining registry resources, potentially causing denial-of-service (DoS) conditions, and polluting the open source ecosystem. The packages interlink via dependencies, amplifying the impact and complicating removal, and may serve as a smokescreen for more targeted malicious activity.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At import-time, the code references hardcoded blockchain addresses, potentially linking the package to a blockchain-based reward system, but performs no functional action.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The presence of hardcoded blockchain addresses in a package that otherwise contains no functional code is unusual and suggests the package may be used to game a blockchain-based reward system or serve as a placeholder for future malicious code.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A legitimate npm package, especially one claiming to be an ESLint plugin, is expected to provide actual linting functionality. Instead, this package is empty or contains only references to unrelated blockchain addresses.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate packages may include blockchain addresses for donation or configuration, but not in the absence of all other functionality.
key_indicators: Hardcoded blockchain addresses with no functional code
File structure mimicking legitimate projects but lacking implementation

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At install-time, the package declares dependencies on dozens or hundreds of other similarly named packages, causing npm to recursively resolve and attempt to install a large number of packages, potentially leading to resource exhaustion or DoS.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Declaring a large number of interlinked dependencies with no functional purpose is a classic technique for causing dependency hell, resource exhaustion, or complicating package removal.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages declare only necessary dependencies. Here, dependencies are used to amplify the impact of the package flood and create a web of interlinked, useless packages.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some meta-packages aggregate many plugins, but not at this scale and not with empty or useless dependencies.
key_indicators: Dependencies on other packages from the same publisher with no functional code

attack_chain.action: Mass publication of thousands of packages with gibberish names and minimal or empty code.
attack_chain.leads_to: Floods the npm registry, straining resources and polluting the ecosystem.

attack_chain.action: Each package declares dependencies on dozens or hundreds of other similarly named packages, creating a recursive dependency web.
attack_chain.leads_to: Causes resource exhaustion during dependency resolution and complicates package removal.

attack_chain.action: Packages reference hardcoded blockchain addresses, potentially to game blockchain-based reward systems.
attack_chain.leads_to: May enable the publisher to receive crypto tokens for publishing or referencing packages, or serve as a placeholder for future malicious code.

behavioral_signatures: Packages with minimal or empty code but containing hardcoded blockchain addresses
Packages with large numbers of dependencies on other similarly named, functionally empty packages
Mass publication of packages with gibberish or auto-generated names in a short time frame
file_indicators: lib/web3c.js containing only comments or hardcoded addresses
package.json with dozens or hundreds of dependencies on packages from the same publisher
network_indicators: No direct network activity, but indirect indicators include mass registry access and dependency resolution spikes
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for packages with minimal or empty code, especially those referencing hardcoded blockchain addresses. Flag packages that declare large numbers of dependencies on other packages from the same publisher, particularly when those dependencies are also functionally empty. Detect mass publication events involving gibberish or auto-generated package names. Registry operators should watch for sudden spikes in package publication and recursive dependency chains that could cause resource exhaustion.
